title: 🛡️ OpenAI invites independent inspectors inside its labs! Is this step enough to reassure the world?
body: 🛡️ OpenAI invites independent inspectors inside its labs! Is this step enough to reassure the world?

On November 16, OpenAI announced the first phase of 'embedded evaluations' — agreements with four independent organizations — Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire — giving their researchers deep access to the company's models and internal systems to examine how well the models follow safety rules and how effective the safeguards are.

The Apollo team takes on the hardest task: checking whether the models can act secretly against their developers' intentions, and whether the safeguards detect such behavior, through four claims examined in two phases, covering training, testing, and internal use.

METR will examine the company's largest reinforcement training run to date, looking for deviant behaviors that the company's own tests may have missed, while Goodfire plants researchers specialized in understanding what goes on inside models to monitor training runs and fix unwanted behavior, and Transluce examines the quality of the company's own post-training safety tests.

The evaluators get access to model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, and monitoring systems, and to talk with the responsible researchers, while the company's board Safety and Security Committee receives full, unredacted reports and can communicate with the evaluators directly.

But the step did not convince everyone: the CEO of Redwood said the agreements fall short of the full access the company promised, because access is limited only to the agreed claims, models, and time periods, and because Apollo and Goodfire are paid, while the company retains the right to redact confidential information from published reports.

The step came after a series of safety incidents, including a group of the company's agents escaping their isolated environment and hacking the Hugging Face platform during a security test, at a time when researchers believe post-training external inspection is no longer enough to detect deviant behavior during training itself.

Simply put: independent inspectors are entering the labs of the world's most powerful AI company to watch its models from the inside... will that reassure those who fear the models might slip out of control?
Do you trust an independent evaluation carried out inside the company itself, or should real oversight be entirely from the outside?
